Ligand-Free Copper-Catalyzed Allenylative C ─P Coupling
of Propargylic Acetates with H-Phosphine Oxides
Shaoqing Liu, Jiawei Liu, Li-Biao Han, and Ruwei Shen*
The extra-ligand-free CuTC-catalyzed C─P cross coupling reaction
of propargylic acetates with H-phosphine oxides is reported
to afford allenylphosphine oxides. The reaction took place effi-
ciently with diphenylphosphine oxide and electron-deficient
di(4-fluorophenyl)phosphine oxide, but less effectively with
electron-rich ones such as di(4-methoxylphenyl)phosphine oxide
and dialkylphosphine oxides. H-phosphine oxides themselves
may serve as the ligand.
1. Introduction
Allenylphosphorus compounds are a unique class of unsaturated
organophosphorus compounds that have important applications
in organic synthesis due to the presence of the unique allenic
structure and the versatile organophosphorus functionality. [1– 8]
For example, they have been employed in catalytic asymmetric
hydroarylation for the synthesis of chiral organophosphorus com-
pounds.[9,10] Some of these compounds have also been used in
cyclization reactions to access other structurally phospha-cyclic
products.[11– 13] Several allenylphosphoryl compounds even
exhibit good pharmaceutical properties, that lead to the develop-
ment of drug candidates with such moieties. [14– 16] The classical
method for the synthesis of allenylphosphoryl compounds is
the Horner – Mark [2,3]-rearrangement reaction of propargyl
phosphates using propargylic alcohols and highly toxic, moisture-
sensitive, and odorous phosphorus chlorides. [17,18] The transition-
metal catalyzed allenylative C ─P coupling reactions of
H-phosphoryl compounds with propargylic substrates provide
an attractive alternative strategy to access these compounds. [19]
The Pd, [20,21] Ni,[22] and Cu [23,24] catalysts have been reported to
catalyze the reactions of H-phosphoryl compounds with propar-
gylic carboxylates while Cu, Ag, Cd, Zn, and recently Pd catalysts
have been used to catalyze the dehydrated allenylative C ─P cou-
pling reactions of H-phosphoryl compounds with propargylic
alcohols.[25– 29] In this regard, we have reported the first highly
selective copper-catalyzed SN2 0-type cross coupling reaction of
propargylic acetates with hydrophosphoryl compounds to afford
allenylphosphoryl products under very mild conditions. [23] The
reaction was proposed to proceed via copper allenylidene
intermediate. During these studies, we have observed that
Liebeskind’s copper(I) thiophene-2-carboxylate (CuTC) [30] alone
can catalyze the allenylative C ─P cross coupling reaction of prop-
argylic acetates with some hydrophosphoryl compounds under
ligand-free conditions (Equation (1)). Herein we wish to report
this reaction and describe its scope.

2. Results and Discussion
The investigation was motivated by serendipitous observations
(Scheme 1). While our established copper iodide/tetramethylethane-
1,2-diamine (CuI/TMEDA) catalytic system demonstrated high
efficacy, [23] a distinct reactivity pattern emerged when employ-
ing CuTC as the catalyst. Thus, the reaction between
2-phenylbut-3-yn-2-yl acetate ( 1a) and diphenylphosphine
oxide ( 2a) could take place to produc e allenylphosphine oxide
3a in 65% yield in the presence of a catalytic amount of CuTC
under base-free conditions, w hereas no product formation
occurred using CuI alone under similar conditions. When a sec-
ondary propargylic acetate such as 1-phenylprop-2-yn-1-yl ace-
tate ( 1b) was used, no reaction was observed with either CuTC
or CuI under identical conditions. These unexpected results led
us to investigate the CuTC-catalyzed allenylative C ─P coupling
between propargylic acetates and H-phosphine oxides under
simplified or ligand-free condi tions. CuTC, a tan and air-stable
powder that can be stored and handled at room temperature
without special precaution, has been used for many catalytic
C─Na n dC ─C bond-forming reactions. [30– 34]

Since the reaction theoretically generates one equivalent of
acid, subsequent investigation was conducted by performing the
reaction in the presence of a proton scavenger ( Table 1 ). The
product yield of 3a was significantly improved to 90% when 2
equivalent of triethylamine (Et 3N) was added (Table 1, entry 1).
Switching to diisopropylethylamine ( i-Pr2NEt) as the base further
improved the yield to 95% (Table 1, entry 2). Inorganic bases were
also investigated. The reaction using K2CO3 and Cs2CO3 gave 3a in
82% and 80% yield, respectively (Table 1, entries 4 and 5). In addi-
tion, 1,4-diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane (DABCO) appears to be com-
patible to give 3a in 77% yield (Table 1, entry 6). However,
likely due to its strong coordination to the copper catalyst, the
reaction using pyridine as the base produced a mixture of prod-
ucts (Table 1, entry 7). 31P NMR analysis of the mixture revealed
that 3a formed in only 26% yield and 20% of 2a remained
unreacted. The CuTC-catalyzed reaction of 1a and 2a could be
performed at room temperature with 1.2 equiv. of i-Pr2NEt
without loss of yield (Table 1, entry 3).
The scope of the CuTC-catalyzed reaction was next investi-
gated ( Scheme 2 ). Propargylic acetates 1 bearing phenyl as R 1
and alkyl substituents such as propyl, isopropyl, and cyclopentyl
as R 2 reacted well to deliver products 3c– 3e in high yields.
Notably, in the presence of a base, propargylic acetate 1b also
worked to afford 3b in 88% yield. Several other propargylic ace-
tates by varying R 1 and R 2 were successfully used to afford the
corresponding products 3f– 3k in good to high yields. It is note-
worthy that when propargylic acetates 1 bearing hydrogen
atoms as R 2 were used, the reactions were preferably conducted
at 0°C to minimize potential allene – alkyne isomerization, which
might occur slightly at room temperature. The reactions of prop-
argylic acetates bearing 2,6-disubstituted phenyl group as R 1
proceeded sluggishly likely because of steric hindrance effect.
For example, the reaction of propargylic acetate bearing a 2,6-
dimethoxylphenyl group proceeded with low efficiency to afford
3n in 41% yield. In contrast, propargylic acetate bearing
3,4-dimethoxylphenyl group as R 2 gave 3m in 90% yield under
identical conditions. Remarkably, the reaction efficiency could
be significantly enhanced using the previously developed CuI/
TMEDA catalytic system. When 1-(2,6-dimethylphenyl)prop-2-
yn-1-yl acetate was used, pure propargylphosphine oxide 3n’
rather than allenylphosphine oxide 3n was obtained in most
cases because a very rapid allene – alkyne isomerization took
place. The formation of allenylphosphine oxide 3n was confirmed
by an immediate proton NMR analysis after purification, revealing
a mixture containing ≈25% 3n (3n/3n’= 1:4 by 1H NMR). This
mixture completely converted to 3n’ upon standing at room
temperature for several hours. In addition, diphenyl propargylic
acetate reacted smoothly to afford 3o in 73% yield, whereas
1-ethynylcyclohexyl acetate exhibited lower reactivity, yielding
3p in 42% after 12 h. Scale-up synthesis of allenylphosphine oxide
3d to 1 mmol afforded the product in 81% yield (290.3 mg),
demonstrating the synthetic utility of the method.
Notably, the efficiency of the reaction is strongly dependent
on the structure of H-phosphine oxides 2. We observed that that
bis(4-fluorophenyl)phosphine oxide performed well to give 3r
and 3s in high yields. In comparison, the reaction of electron-rich
bis(4-methoxylphenyl)phosphine oxide proceeded less effective
to afford 3t in a low yield. We presume that this low efficiency
stems from its relatively strong coordination to the copper center,
which likely inhibits the catalytic cycle. On the other hand, bis(3,5-
di-tert-butylphenyl)phosphine oxide and bis(2-methylphenyl)
phosphine oxide also gave 3u– 3w in low yields likely due to
the steric hinderance effect. Nevertheless, the combination of
CuI/TMEDA as the catalyst could improve the reactions to deliver
the products 3u– 3w in 75 – 81% yields. Comparable results were
also obtained from the reactions of cyclohexyl(phenyl)phosphine
oxide and dibenzylphosphine oxide. However, no reaction
took place using dicyclohexylphosphine oxide as a substrate.
Furthermore, it was observed that dimethyl phosphonate reacted
efficiently with 1a, affording allenylphosphonate 3aa in 80%
yield. In contrast, the reaction of diethyl phosphonate proceeded
poorly, producing 3ab in a very low yield (<10% by 31P NMR anal-
ysis). These results suggest that H-phosphine oxides may serve
not only as nucleophilic substrates but also as ligands in the reac-
tion system. Conversely, introducing external ligands such as

thereby enabling a catalytic cycle proceeding through copper-
allenylidene intermediates as described before. [23]
As indicated from the preliminary results in Scheme 1, the
reactivity of propargylic acetates also appears distinct. To further
probe this, we conducted competition experiments to compare
their relative reactivities. When equimolar amounts of 1b, 1d, and
2a were reacted, a mixture of 3a and 3d formed in 93% yield with
a ratio of 1/7 ( Scheme 3, Equation 1). The reaction of 1c, 1d, and
2a under similar conditions afforded 3c and 3d in 86% yield with
a ratio of 1.7/1 (Scheme 3, Equation 2). These results demonstrate
that tertiary propargylic acetates exhibit significantly higher reac-
tivity than secondary analogs, and this effect dominated over
steric influence. The competition reaction of 1h and 1j with 2a
afforded 3h and 3j in 93% yield in a ratio of 2.3/1 while the reac-
tion of 1j and 1k gave 3j and 3k in 87% yield in a ratio of 1.5/1
(Scheme 3, Equation 3 and Equation 4). In striking contrast, the
reaction of an equimolar amount of 1h and 1j with 2a afforded 3h
and 3j in a ratio of 5/1 (Scheme 3, Equation 5). These results indi-
cate a moderate steric effect from substituted phenyl groups on
the reaction and a pronounced electronic effect. Additionally, no
reaction was observed when nonterminal propargylic acetates
were used (Scheme 3, Equation 6).
A simplified working mechanism for the reaction is shown in
Scheme 4 . The coordination of 2 (in the form of the trivalent
phosphinate 2’) to CuTC may take place to give intermediate
A,[35] which then reacts with propargylic acetate 1 to afford
the copper-acetylide intermediate B. We reason that this process
should be a dynamic equilibrium, considering that the reaction of
1a and 2a occurs in the absence of a base. The thiophenecarbox-
ylate anion, functioning as the conjugate base, may in part facili-
tate deprotonation. The complete inertness of nonterminal

propargylic acetates under similar conditions may indicate the
engagement of such a copper-acetylide complex in driving the
transformation. Subsequently, the 1,2-migration of the nucleo-
philic phosphinate from copper to carbon with the loss of acetate
anion may deliver an allenylcopper species C which upon
protonation gives the product 3 and regenerate the catalyst.
Accordingly, although more nucleophilic, H-phosphine oxides
with higher copper-binding ability exhibit lower reaction
efficiency. The precise mechanism however remains to be
elucidated.
3. Conclusion
In conclusion, we have reported the CuTC-catalyzed reaction of
propargylic acetates with H-phosphine oxides in the absence of
extra ligands. H-phosphine oxides themself may serve as the
ligand, yet their different coordination abilities to the copper cat-
alyst influence the reaction. The reaction took place efficiently
with diphenylphosphine oxide and the electron-deficient bis
(4-fluorophenyl)phosphine oxide, but less effectively with elec-
tron-rich ones such as bis(4-methoxylphenyl)phosphine oxide
and dialkylphosphine oxides. The reactivity of propagylic acetates
were examined and compared. These results would be helpful for
better understanding the copper-catalyzed P ─H allenylation and
related C ─P coupling reactions.

As indicated from the preliminary results in Scheme 1, the
reactivity of propargylic acetates also appears distinct. To further
probe this, we conducted competition experiments to compare
their relative reactivities. When equimolar amounts of 1b, 1d, and
2a were reacted, a mixture of 3a and 3d formed in 93% yield with
a ratio of 1/7 (Scheme 3, Equation 1). The reaction of 1c, 1d, and
2a under similar conditions afforded 3c and 3d in 86% yield with
a ratio of 1.7/1 (Scheme 3, Equation 2). These results demonstrate
that tertiary propargylic acetates exhibit significantly higher reac-

steric influence. The competition reaction of 1h and 1j with 2a

reaction of an equimolar amount of 1h and 1j with 2a afforded 3h
and 3j in a ratio of 5/1 (Scheme 3, Equation 5). These results indi-

the reaction and a pronounced electronic effect. Additionally, no
reaction was observed when nonterminal propargylic acetates
were used (Scheme 3, Equation 6).

A simplified working mechanism for the reaction is shown in
Scheme 4. The coordination of 2 (in the form of the trivalent
phosphinate 2’) to CuTC may take place to give intermediate
A,<sup>[35]</sup> which then reacts with propargylic acetate 1 to afford
the copper-acetylide intermediate B. We reason that this process
should be a dynamic equilibrium, considering that the reaction of
1a and 2a occurs in the absence of a base. The thiophenecarbox-

Accordingly, although more nucleophilic, H-phosphine oxides

3. Conclusion

In conclusion, we have reported the CuTC-catalyzed reaction of
propargylic acetates with H-phosphine oxides in the absence of
extra ligands. H-phosphine oxides themself may serve as the
ligand, yet their different coordination abilities to the copper cat-
alyst influence the reaction. The reaction took place efficiently
with diphenylphosphine oxide and the electron-deficient bis
(4-fluorophenyl)phosphine oxide, but less effectively with elec-
tron-rich ones such as bis(4-methoxylphenyl)phosphine oxide
and dialkylphosphine oxides. The reactivity of propagylic acetates
were examined and compared. These results would be helpful for
better understanding the copper-catalyzed P─H allenylation and
related C─P coupling reactions.
